title: The reed, again
hookLine: the reed's longing, now heard with years of practice behind you (Masnavi 1)
tomorrow: a scholar, a boatman, a storm. who's laughing now?

cards: A song comes on in the car, one your parents played when you were small, and something in your chest goes tight. Or you stand in your own bedroom and miss it, though you haven't left yet.
Homesick for a place you're still in. Early on this path you heard Rumi's reed flute for the first time, cut from its reed-bed and crying. The reed hasn't stopped.
Heard again, with all these days of practice behind you, what is it saying now?

teach.h: THE NEY: CUT FROM THE REED-BED.
teach.b: The Masnavi, Rumi's long poem, opens with the ney, the reed flute. Paraphrased: listen to the reed, how it tells a story, complaining of separation. Ever since I was cut from the reed-bed, my cry has made people weep.
Then come three lines worth hearing again, now. First: whoever is far from their root keeps looking for the time of union.
The ache isn't a malfunction. It's a compass, pointing back. Second: the reed wants a chest torn by separation, so it can tell someone the pain of longing.

teach.h: ONLY THE TORN CAN HEAR IT.
teach.b: Only those who've missed something can really hear it. Your own homesickness is what lets you understand someone else's.

teach.h: THE FIRE OF LOVE IN THE REED.
teach.b: Third: the poem says it's the fire of love that has fallen into the reed. The sound isn't sadness alone.
Rumi's readers hear the reed as the soul, cut from its origin with God and longing to return; some also hear Rumi's own grief for his lost friend Shams. Either way, the cry is the music.
A reed that stopped longing would just be a stick. So when the old song plays in the car, or the room you haven't left already feels like a memory, Rumi wouldn't rush you past it. He'd say: listen.
That ache is how the reed sings.

how: The opening lines of the Masnavi, the Song of the Reed, are recited and sung in Persian and in translation; in Mevlevi gatherings the ney flute is played, and its breathy sound is heard as the reed's longing.

o: a sadness you should cure as fast as you can
a regret about leaving a place by choice
a longing for home that is itself the music

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: where the reed was cut from
a longing for the time of union
the one who can hear the song

s: the reed cries because it's broken
it cries because it was cut from its reed-bed. the cry is the music.
in the opening, the reed seeks a heart torn by separation to tell its longing to
only someone who has missed something can really hear it.
in Rumi's poem, longing is a problem to get rid of quickly
the ache is a compass pointing home; a reed that stopped longing would be a stick.

games.q: a friend whose family moved here last year goes quiet at lunch when a song from home plays. what would the reed do?
o: ask about the song, and let him tell you about home.
switch the music fast so he doesn't have to feel sad.
remind him he'll stop missing home in a few months.
games.why: the reed looks for someone who knows separation, to tell its longing to. listening is the reed's answer.

practice: Breathe in slowly, all the way down, then hum one long, low note for as long as the breath lasts. Listen to it fade, and listen to the quiet after it.
Do it once or twice more, letting the sound carry whatever you're missing right now.

wordCard.voice: The reed: Rumi's ney, cut from its reed-bed, whose cry of separation opens the Masnavi and turns longing into music.

orig.note: Persian: the reed-bed, the marsh the reed was cut from.

carryVoice: For the drive home: the longing is the song, and a reed that stopped aching would be a stick. One story of Rumi's eight.

sources.ref: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1, opening verses (the Song of the Reed)
